title: Is the table real? The two truths
carry: two truths: it works, yet doesn't stand alone
tomorrow: point to your body. where exactly is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday: for the sake of wisdom. Every practice points somewhere. For wisdom. Now, the first thing wisdom sees.

Knock on a table. Solid. It holds your coffee, your laptop, your elbows at dinner. Now take away the legs, the top, the screws, the wood, and the word table we all agreed on. What's left over? Nothing. It's an odd question to ask about furniture. It's also a real one. So is the table real or not? Shantideva's answer: yes, and it depends which truth you're asking.
screen: `KNOCK ON A TABLE.` → `TAKE AWAY THE PARTS.` → `REAL, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: He says there are two truths: the conventional and the ultimate. Conventional truth is the world as it works. Tables hold cups, names call people, kindness helps. Ultimate truth is how things are when you look all the way down, and there he says something startling: the ultimate is not within reach of the intellect, because the intellect itself belongs to the conventional. Neither truth cancels the other. The table really holds your cup. And it isn't a thing standing on its own apart from its parts and our naming. A neighbor tradition says something close. The old Chinese book of the Tao, in James Legge's English: "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao." Shared ground: words and ideas reach only so far; what's deepest is beyond what we can name. One honest difference. The book speaks of the nameless Tao as the origin of heaven and earth, a source. Shantideva's ultimate isn't a source things come from; it's that nothing stands on its own. Two maps of the edge of words. Two truths.
screen: `CONVENTIONAL AND ULTIMATE.` · `BEYOND THE REACH OF THE INTELLECT.` · `THE TAO THAT CAN BE TRODDEN.` · `SAME EDGE, DIFFERENT MAP.` · then, large: `TWO TRUTHS.`

segments.voice: Pick up or look at one ordinary thing near you: a mug, a pen, your phone. First describe it the everyday way, in a sentence: what it is and what it's for. Then look again and name its parts one by one, and notice there's no extra piece called mug among them. Hold both views at once.
Two truths: the conventional and the ultimate. Things work as they seem, and they aren't what they seem.
The line to hold: two truths; the cup holds coffee, and doesn't stand on its own. Forty-two days into the guide.

chat.says: ông says his juniper is the same tree he planted and also brand new every spring. both true??
options: both, two ways: by name it's his tree; up close, it's parts always changing.
only the second. the 'same tree' part is just an illusion to drop.
only the first. spring growth is just leaves; the real tree never changes.
chat.meaning: Shantideva's two truths: conventionally it's Ông's juniper; ultimately it's changing parts, with no fixed tree apart from them. Neither cancels the other.

tie.story: Shantideva teaches two truths: the conventional and the ultimate, and neither cancels the other.
